MODEL / 01

Black–Scholes–Merton estimates a theoretical option value from six inputs. Change an assumption and observe how the value and sensitivities change. This calculator uses hypothetical inputs; it does not use an option chain or recommend a trade.

How sensitive is the value?

These are model derivatives at the chosen inputs, not estimates of future profit.

Measure Call Put

Delta: value change per $1 underlying move. Gamma: delta change per $1. Vega: value change per 1 percentage-point volatility move. Theta: value change per calendar day. Rho: value change per 1 percentage-point rate move. These are local sensitivities, not exact outcomes for large changes.

MODEL NOTES

What the calculation assumes.

The model prices European options, exercisable only at expiry. It assumes constant volatility and risk-free rate, a continuous dividend yield, and frictionless trading. Actual options have changing volatility, bid/ask spreads, and other market effects. A theoretical price is not a tradable quote or a historical backtest.

The displayed prices use call = S·e−qT·N(d₁) − K·e−rT·N(d₂) and put–call parity call − put = S·e−qT − K·e−rT. The implementation has tests for a standard numerical benchmark, parity, Greeks, and limiting behavior. Read the original paper ↗ or the source code ↗.

To study historical options trading, Orion would need point-in-time contract chains, executable prices, and an explicit entry, exit, and cost model. That work is separate from this calculator. Return to strategy backtesting ↗
